label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
	There is a $C^\infty$ embedded open annulus $M\subset\mathbb R^3$ with strictly negative Gaussian curvature and an injective Gauss map $N:M\to\mathbb S^2$, containing a smooth regular simple closed asymptotic curve $\gamma$ with
	\[
		\operatorname{Lk}(\gamma,N\circ\gamma)=0.
	\]
head: environment

label: cor:binormal
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:binormal}
	There are smooth regular embeddings $\gamma:\mathbb S^1\to\mathbb R^3$ and $n:\mathbb S^1\to\mathbb S^2$ such that
	\[
		\langle n,\gamma'\rangle=\langle n,\gamma''\rangle=0,\qquad\operatorname{Lk}(\gamma,n)=0.
	\]
head: environment

label: add:lem:tangent-lines
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{add:lem:tangent-lines}
	Suppose that $P,Q:\mathbb T\to\mathbb R^2$ are smooth regular closed curves, $Q'=fP'$ with $f>0$, and $I(P,Q)=0$. The tangent lines of $P$ cover $\mathbb R^2$, as do the tangent lines of $Q$. In particular, neither curve is locally star-shaped, and neither can be the boundary of a convex domain.
head: environment

label: add:eq:weighted-period
title: Proof
body_md:
Integration by parts gives $I(P,Q)=\int_0^{24}\det(P,Q')\,\mathrm d t$. Since both curves are closed, for every $a,b\in\mathbb R^2$ we have
	\[
		\begin{aligned}
			I(P,Q)&=\int_0^{24}f(t)\det(P(t)-a,P'(t))dt,\\
			I(P,Q)&=\int_0^{24}\frac{1}{f(t)}\det(Q(t)-b,Q'(t))dt.
		\end{aligned}
		\refstepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{add:eq:weighted-period}
	\]
	Indeed, the terms containing $a$ and $b$ vanish because
	\[
	\int_0^{24}fP'=\int_0^{24}Q'=0\quad\text{and}\quad\int_0^{24}f^{-1}Q'=\int_0^{24}P'=0.
	\]
	If $a$ lies on no tangent line of $P$, then $\det(P-a,P')$ is continuous and never zero. It therefore has a fixed sign, contradicting the first identity in \eqref{add:eq:weighted-period} and $f>0$. The second identity proves the same assertion for $Q$. Finally, an interior point of a convex domain lies on none of the tangent lines to its smooth boundary.

label: prop:planar
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $L\in[43,44]$, consider the polygons with cyclic vertices $p_i=p_i(L)$ and $q_i$ in Table~\ref{tab:vertices}. The edge directions are $E=(1,0)$, $S=(0,-1)$, $N=(0,1)$, and $W=(-1,0)$. Indices are taken modulo $12$.
	
\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\renewcommand{1.15}{1.15}
\begin{tabular}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
$i$ & $p_i$ & $q_i$ & $e_i$ & $a_i$ & $b_i$\\ \hline
0 & $(0,0)$ & $(0,0)$ & $E$ & $L$ & $2$\\
1 & $(L,0)$ & $(2,0)$ & $S$ & $1$ & $1$\\
2 & $(L,-1)$ & $(2,-1)$ & $E$ & $1$ & $4$\\
3 & $(L+1,-1)$ & $(6,-1)$ & $N$ & $21/10$ & $4$\\
4 & $(L+1,11/10)$ & $(6,3)$ & $W$ & $1$ & $1$\\
5 & $(L,11/10)$ & $(5,3)$ & $S$ & $1$ & $7/2$\\
6 & $(L,1/10)$ & $(5,-1/2)$ & $W$ & $L$ & $2$\\
7 & $(0,1/10)$ & $(3,-1/2)$ & $N$ & $1$ & $5/2$\\
8 & $(0,11/10)$ & $(3,2)$ & $W$ & $1$ & $5$\\
9 & $(-1,11/10)$ & $(-2,2)$ & $S$ & $21/10$ & $5$\\
10 & $(-1,-1)$ & $(-2,-3)$ & $E$ & $1$ & $2$\\
11 & $(0,-1)$ & $(0,-3)$ & $N$ & $1$ & $3$
\end{tabular}
\caption{The vertices and edge lengths of the two polygons: $p_{i+1}-p_i=a_i e_i$ and $q_{i+1}-q_i=b_i e_i$.}
\label{tab:vertices}
\end{table}

	Both polygons are simple, with separation bounds independent of $L$. For the first polygon, the two long horizontal edges lie at heights $0$ and $1/10$. The other edges lie in the rectangles
	\[
		[-1,0]\times[-1,11/10],\qquad[L,L+1]\times[-1,11/10].
	\]
	The vertical portions on each of the lines $x=0$ and $x=L$ are separated by a gap of $1/10$. It follows by comparing the edges that nonadjacent edges are at distance at least $1/10$, as is any vertex from a nonincident edge. For the second polygon, the horizontal and vertical edges are listed below by their supporting coordinates and intervals:
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrr}
\text{height}&0&-1&3&-1/2&2&-3\\
\text{interval}&[0,2]&[2,6]&[5,6]&[3,5]&[-2,3]&[-2,0],\\[3pt]
\text{abscissa}&2&6&5&3&-2&0\\
\text{interval}&[-1,0]&[-1,3]&[-1/2,3]&[-1/2,2]&[-3,2]&[-3,0].
\end{array}
\]
	These intervals give the corresponding separation bound $1/2$. Adjacent edges of either polygon are orthogonal and meet only at their common vertex. We round corresponding corners in the same way. Choose a nonnegative smooth function $w$, supported in $[1/4,3/4]$ and symmetric about $1/2$, with $\int_0^1w=\pi/2$. Set
	\[
		\theta(u)=\int_0^u w(s)ds,\qquad h=\int_0^1\cos\theta(u)du,\qquad c=h^{-1}.
	\]
	Symmetry gives $\theta(1-u)=\pi/2-\theta(u)$, so $\int_0^1\sin\theta=h$. Since $\cos\theta+\sin\theta\geq1$, we have $c\leq2$. At the $i$-th corner use the arc
	\[
		r_i(u)=-e_{i-1}+c\int_0^u\left(\cos\theta(s)e_{i-1}+\sin\theta(s)e_i\right)ds,\qquad 0\leq u\leq1.\refstepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq:rounding}
	\]
	It satisfies
	\[
		r_i(0)=-e_{i-1},\qquad r_i(1)=e_i,\qquad |r_i'|=c.
	\]
	Near its endpoints, the velocity is respectively $ce_{i-1}$ and $ce_i$. In the orthonormal basis $(e_{i-1},e_i)$, the two coordinates of $r_i$ lie in $[-1,0]\times[0,1]$, and their sum is strictly increasing. Thus $r_i$ is simple and $|r_i|\leq\sqrt2$.\par
	Fix $\delta=1/100$. Replace the corners at $p_i$ and $q_i$ by $p_i+\delta r_i$ and $q_i+\delta r_i$, and retain the straight edges between their endpoints. The disks of radius $2\delta$ about the vertices of either polygon are disjoint and meet no nonincident edge. Each replacement arc lies in its vertex disk and, by the coordinate monotonicity just noted, meets its retained incident edges only at the endpoints. The rounded curves are therefore simple. Give each corner and the following straight segment a parameter interval of length $1$. On a corner use the parametrization above. On the $i$th straight segment choose a smooth nonnegative function $\psi$, compactly supported in $(0,1)$ with $\int_0^1\psi=1$, and prescribe the velocities
	\[
		\begin{aligned}
			P'&=\alpha_i(u)e_i,&
			\alpha_i(u)&=\delta c+(a_i-2\delta-\delta c)\psi(u),\\
			Q'&=\beta_i(u)e_i,&
			\beta_i(u)&=\delta c+(b_i-2\delta-\delta c)\psi(u).
		\end{aligned}
	\]
	Their integrals are $a_i-2\delta$ and $b_i-2\delta$, the lengths of the retained edges. Since $a_i,b_i\geq1$ and $c\leq2$, both speeds are positive. Near every join the velocities agree and are constant, so the resulting periodic parametrizations $P$ and $Q$ are smooth and regular. On corners $Q'=P'$, and on straight segments $Q'=(\beta_i/\alpha_i)P'$. Hence $Q'=fP'$ for a smooth positive function $f$, equal to $1$ near all joins. It remains to choose $L$ so that the mixed integral vanishes. For the polygons before rounding, its value is
	\[
		\begin{aligned}
			I_0(L)&=\sum_{i=0}^{11}a_i\det(q_i,e_i)\\
			&=0-2+1+\frac{63}{5}+3-5-\frac L2+3+2+\frac{21}{5}+3+0\\
			&=\frac{109}{5}-\frac L2.
		\end{aligned}
		\refstepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq:polygon-period}
	\]
	This is independent of the speeds along corresponding edges, since displacement along an edge of $Q$ is parallel to $dP$. For the rounded curves, the $i$th straight segment contributes $(a_i-2\delta)\det(q_i,e_i)$, while the $i$th corner contributes
	\[
		\delta\det(q_i,e_{i-1}+e_i)+\delta^2\int_0^1\det(r_i,r_i')du.
	\]
	The terms linear in $\delta$ cancel because
	\[
		\sum_i\det(q_i,e_{i-1})=\sum_i\det(q_{i-1},e_{i-1})=\sum_i\det(q_i,e_i).
	\]
	The first equality uses $q_i-q_{i-1}=b_{i-1}e_{i-1}$. Consequently,
	\[
		I_\delta(L)=\frac{109}{5}-\frac L2+\delta^2C,\qquad C=\sum_{i=0}^{11}\int_0^1\det(r_i,r_i')du.\refstepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq:smooth-period}
	\]
	The constant $C$ is independent of $L$, and
	\[
		|C|\leq12\sqrt2\,c\leq24\sqrt2<36.
	\]
	Choose
	\[
		L_*=\frac{218}{5}+2\delta^2C.\refstepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq:L-choice}
	\]
	Then $|L_*-218/5|<0.0072$, so $L_*\in[43,44]$ and all the preceding separation and regularity estimates apply. Equation \eqref{eq:smooth-period} gives $I_\delta(L_*)=0$, as required.
head: environment

label: lem:ribbon
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ribbon}
	Let $\gamma:\mathbb S^1\to\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth regular embedding, and let $V(t,r)$, $0\leq r\leq1$, be a smooth family of vector fields along $\gamma$. Suppose that $\gamma'(t)$ and $V(t,r)$ are linearly independent for every $(t,r)$. There is $a>0$, independent of $r$, such that
	\[
		F_r(t,u)=\gamma(t)+uV(t,r)
	\]
	is a smooth embedding of $\mathbb S^1\times[-a,a]$ for every $r$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The rank condition holds along $u=0$, hence on a uniform strip by compactness. If there were no uniform injective strip, we could find $r_j\to r_0$ and distinct pairs $(t_j,u_j),(s_j,v_j)$ with $u_j,v_j\to0$ and equal $F_{r_j}$-images. Passing to subsequences gives $t_j\to t_0$ and $s_j\to s_0$. The limiting equality $\gamma(t_0)=\gamma(s_0)$ implies $t_0=s_0$. Choose a linear projection $\pi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ that is injective on the plane spanned by $\gamma'(t_0)$ and $V(t_0,r_0)$. In a local coordinate on the circle, the map
	\[
		(t,u,r)\longmapsto\left(\pi F_r(t,u),r\right)
	\]
	has invertible differential at $(t_0,0,r_0)$. The inverse function theorem contradicts the chosen collisions. At $r_0=0$ or $1$, apply it after a local smooth extension in $r$. Thus a uniform strip is injective. Since the closed strip is compact, each restriction is an embedding.
head: environment

label: lem:normal-neighborhood
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:normal-neighborhood}
	Let $Y$ be a smooth surface and $H:\mathbb S^1\times(-b,b)\to Y$ a smooth map. If $H(t,0)$ is injective in $t$ and $DH$ has rank two along $u=0$, then $H$ is an injective immersion on $\mathbb S^1\times[-a,a]$ for some $0<a<b$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Compactness gives the rank condition on a smaller strip. If no smaller strip were injective, collisions would converge to a pair of points of the core with the same image. Injectivity on the core makes their limits equal, contradicting the inverse function theorem in a surface chart at that point.
head: environment

label: prop:annulus
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:orthogonality
title: Proof
body_md:
The zero integral in~\eqref{eq:planar-data} makes $z$ smooth and periodic. Since $P$ is a regular embedding, so is $\gamma$. The map
	\[
		\Phi(q)=\frac{(-Jq,1)}{\sqrt{1+|q|^2}}
	\]
	is a diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R^2$ to the upper open hemisphere, with inverse $\xi\mapsto J(\xi_1,\xi_2)/\xi_3$. Thus $n=\Phi\circ Q$ is a regular embedded spherical curve and $n_3>0$. The definition of $z$ gives
	\[
		\langle n,\gamma'\rangle=0,\qquad\langle n,\gamma''\rangle=\frac{\det(Q',P')}{\sqrt{1+|Q|^2}}=0.\refstepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq:orthogonality}
	\]
	It follows that $n'$ is orthogonal to both $n$ and $T$, so $n'=\lambda\nu$. In fact,
	\[
		\lambda=-\frac{fv}{1+|Q|^2}<0.\refstepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq:lambda}
	\]
	To check this, put $W=(-JQ,1)$ and $w=|W|$. Since $W\perp\gamma'$ and $Q'=fP'$, a scalar triple product gives
	\[
		\langle W',W\times\gamma'\rangle=-f|\gamma'|^2,\qquad\langle n',\nu\rangle=\frac{\langle W',W\times\gamma'\rangle}{w^2v}=-\frac{fv}{w^2}.
	\]
	No assumption on the ordinary curvature of $\gamma$ enters this computation. Along $u=0$ we have $F_t=vT$, $F_u=\nu$, and $F_t\times F_u=vn$. Lemma \ref{lem:ribbon} therefore gives an embedded closed strip. On a neighborhood of a sufficiently small such strip, its unit normal is
	\[
		\mathcal N(t,u)=\frac{F_t\times F_u}{|F_t\times F_u|},\qquad\mathcal N(t,0)=n(t).
	\]
	At the core, the first fundamental form is $\operatorname{diag}(v^2,1)$, and the second fundamental coefficients are
	\[
		\mathrm{II}_{tt}=\langle\gamma'',n\rangle=0,\qquad\mathrm{II}_{tu}=\langle\nu',n\rangle=-\lambda,\qquad\mathrm{II}_{uu}=0.
	\]
	Hence the core is asymptotic, and
	\[
		K(t,0)=-\frac{\lambda^2}{v^2}=-\frac{f(t)^2}{(1+|Q(t)|^2)^2}<0.\refstepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq:negative-curvature}
	\]
	By compactness, $K<0$ on a uniform smaller strip. To obtain injectivity of the Gauss map on the whole strip, write $\nu'=bT-\lambda n$. Differentiating the normalized cross product at the core gives
	\[
		\mathcal N_t(t,0)=\lambda\nu,\qquad\mathcal N_u(t,0)=\frac{\lambda}{v}T.\refstepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq:gauss-derivatives}
	\]
	Indeed, $\partial_u(F_t\times F_u)=\nu'\times\nu=bn+\lambda T$; normalization removes the component parallel to $n$ and divides the remaining component by $v$. The two derivatives in \eqref{eq:gauss-derivatives} are independent. Since $\mathcal N(t,0)=n(t)$ is injective, Lemma \ref{lem:normal-neighborhood} makes $\mathcal N$ injective on a smaller closed strip. Choose $a>0$ so that all these conclusions hold. Then $M=F(\mathbb T\times(-a,a))$ is a smooth embedded open annulus, and $N(F(t,u))=\mathcal N(t,u)$ defines the required injective Gauss map on $M$.

label: add:cor:graph
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\pi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ be the horizontal projection. On the core, $\pi F(t,0)=P(t)$, and
	\[
		\det\left((\pi F)_t,(\pi F)_u\right)(t,0)=(F_t\times F_u)_3(t,0)=v(t)n_3(t)>0.
	\]
	Since $P$ is an embedding, Lemma \ref{lem:normal-neighborhood}, applied with target $\mathbb R^2$, shows that $\pi\circ F$ is an injective immersion on a sufficiently small closed strip. Its restriction to the open strip is a diffeomorphism onto a bounded planar annulus $\Omega$. The third coordinate of $F\circ(\pi\circ F)^{-1}$ defines $h$. We may also shrink the strip so that its chosen normal has positive third component. The upward graph normal is then
	\[
		N(x,h(x))=\frac{(-\nabla h(x),1)}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla h(x)|^2}}.
	\]
	The map $p\mapsto(-p,1)/\sqrt{1+|p|^2}$ is a diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R^2$ onto the upper hemisphere. Hence injectivity of the Gauss map implies injectivity of $\nabla h$. The graph curvature formula
	\[
		K(x,h(x))=\frac{\det D^2h(x)}{(1+|\nabla h(x)|^2)^2}
	\]
	gives $\det D^2h<0$ on $\Omega$. Comparing the graph normal with \eqref{eq:lift} gives $\nabla h(P)=JQ$, and differentiating yields
	\[
		D^2h(P)P'=JQ'=fJP'.
	\]
	At each point of $P$, set $E=P'/|P'|$. In the orthonormal basis $(E,JE)$, symmetry of the Hessian therefore gives
	\[
		D^2h(P)=
		\begin{pmatrix}
			0&f\\
			f&\mu
		\end{pmatrix}
	\]
	for some real-valued function $\mu$. Its determinant is $-f^2$, proving \eqref{add:eq:graph-data}.
head: environment

label: lem:zero-linking
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:zero-linking}
	Suppose that $\gamma(t)=(P(t),z(t))$, where $P:\mathbb T\to\mathbb R^2$ is a smooth regular embedding and $z$ is smooth. Let $n:\mathbb T\to\mathbb S^2$ be a smooth field with $\langle n,\gamma'\rangle=0$ and $n_3>0$. Then $\gamma+\varepsilon n$ is a regular embedding disjoint from $\gamma$ for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, and $\operatorname{Lk}(\gamma,n)=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $e_3=(0,0,1)$ and set
	\[
		V(t,r)=(1-r)n(t)+re_3,\qquad 0\leq r\leq1.
	\]
	Since
	\[
		\langle n,V(t,r)\rangle=(1-r)+rn_3(t)>0,
	\]
	each field $V(\cdot,r)$ is transverse to $\gamma'$. Lemma \ref{lem:ribbon} supplies $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that $\gamma$ and $\gamma+\varepsilon V(\cdot,r)$ are disjoint regular embeddings for all $r\in[0,1]$ and $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$. Homotopy invariance of linking therefore gives
	\[
		\operatorname{Lk}(\gamma,\gamma+\varepsilon n)=\operatorname{Lk}(\gamma,\gamma+\varepsilon e_3).
	\]
	For fixed $\varepsilon$ in this interval, flatten the latter pair by
	\[
		\alpha_r(t)=(P(t),(1-r)z(t)),\qquad\beta_r(t)=\alpha_r(t)+\varepsilon e_3,\qquad 0\leq r\leq1.
	\]
	Each component is a regular embedding, since its planar projection is $P$. The two components remain disjoint: equality of their planar coordinates forces equality of the parameters, but their heights then differ by $\varepsilon$. At $r=1$ they lie in two parallel planes and have linking number zero. Another application of homotopy invariance proves the lemma.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Choose $P,Q,f$ from Proposition \ref{prop:planar}, and form the lift \eqref{eq:lift}. Proposition \ref{prop:annulus} gives the embedded negatively curved annulus and its injective Gauss map. Since $P$ is embedded and $n_3>0$, Lemma \ref{lem:zero-linking} gives zero normal self-linking. This proves the theorem. The same $\gamma$ and $n$ satisfy the corollary by \eqref{eq:orthogonality} and the regularity and injectivity of $n$.
head: environment

label: rem:continuous-binormal
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:continuous-binormal}
	To see why regularity of the binormal matters in Corollary \ref{cor:binormal}, consider
	\[
		\gamma_0(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,\cos2t),\qquad b_0(t)=\frac{(-4\cos^3t,4\sin^3t,1)}{\sqrt{1+16(\cos^6t+\sin^6t)}}.
	\]
	The numerator of $b_0$ is $\gamma_0'\times\gamma_0''$, so $b_0$ is a smooth unit binormal. It is injective: dividing its first two coordinates by its third recovers $-4\cos^3t$ and $4\sin^3t$, which determine $t$ modulo $2\pi$. Lemma \ref{lem:zero-linking} gives $\operatorname{Lk}(\gamma_0,b_0)=0$. However, $b_0'(t)=0$ at the four points where $\sin2t=0$, so $b_0$ is not a regular embedding. This is the case $a=1$ of the closed asymptotic curves on the graph $z=x^4-y^4$ in \cite[Section 2]{NZZ}. It answers the continuous-binormal question as stated in \cite[Problem 1.4]{Ghomi}, but not its regular-binormal version.
head: environment
